source_text: Καθάπερ γὰρ οἱ τὴν σωματικὴν ἀθλοῦντες ἄθλησιν, καὶ πρὸ τῶν στεφάνων, καὶ πρὸ τῶν βραβείων ἀπ' αὐτῆς τῆς γυμνασίας καὶ τοῦ παλαίειν μέγαν λαμβάνουσι τὸν μισθὸν, ὑγιεινότερα καὶ δυνατώτερα αὑτῶν τὰ σώματα διὰ τῆς γυμνασίας κατασκευάζοντες, καὶ πᾶσαν διαφεύγοντες ἀῤῥωστίαν· οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀγώνων τῆς ἀρετῆς, καὶ πρὶν ἢ τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνοιγῆναι, καὶ πρὶν ἢ τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ παραγενέσθαι, καὶ πρὶν ἢ τὰς ἀμοιβὰς ἡμᾶς ἀπολαβεῖν, μέγαν ἐντεῦθεν καρπούμεθα τὸν μισθὸν, τῆς ψυχῆς ἡμῖν φιλοσοφωτέρας καθισταμένης. Καὶ γὰρ οἱ πολλὴν πλεύσαντες θάλασσαν, καὶ μυρίων ἀνασχόμενοι κυμάτων, καὶ πολλοῖς θηρίοις πυκτεύσαντες, καὶ πολλοὺς χειμῶνας ἐνεγκόντες, καὶ πρὸ τῆς ἐμπορίας αὐτῆς οὐ μικρὸν ἀπὸ τῆς μακρᾶς ἀποδημίας ταύτης καρποῦνται τὸ κέρδος τῷ θαῤῥεῖν καὶ κατατολμᾷν τοῦ πελάγους, καὶ ἀδεῶς καὶ μεθ' ἡδονῆς τὰς διαποντίους ταύτας ποιεῖσθαι ἀποδημίας· οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος βίου, ὁ πολλὰς ἐνεγκὼν θλίψεις διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν, ὁ πολλὰ δεινὰ παθὼν, καὶ πρὸ τῆς βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν μεγάλην ἔλαβεν ἀμοιβὴν, παῤῥησίαν κτησάμενος πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν ἐντεῦθεν ἤδη, καὶ ὑψηλοτέραν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κατασκευάσας ψυχὴν, ὡς ἁπάντων λοιπὸν καταγελᾷν τῶν δεινῶν. Ἵνα δὲ καὶ σαφέστερον γένηται τὸ λεγόμενον, ἐπὶ παραδείγματος αὐτὸ βούλομαι ποιῆσαι φανερόν. Αὐτὸς γὰρ οὗτος ὁ Παῦλος μυρίων ἀνασχόμενος δεινῶν, οὐ μικρὰς καὶ ἐντεῦθεν ἔλαβε τὰς ἀμοιβὰς, καταγελῶν τυράννων, κατεξανιστάμενος μαινομένων δήμων, πάσης ὑπερορῶν τιμωρίας, καὶ πρὸς θηρία, καὶ πρὸς σίδηρον, καὶ πρὸς πελάγη, καὶ πρὸς κρημνοὺς, καὶ πρὸς ἐπαναστάσεις, καὶ πρὸς ἐπιβουλὰς, καὶ πρὸς ἅπαντα τὰ δεινὰ ἀκατάπληκτος μένων, οὗ τί γένοιτ' ἂν ἴσον; Τὸν μὲν γὰρ ἀγύμναστον καὶ μηδὲν παθόντα δεινὸν καὶ τὰ τυχόντα θορυβεῖν εἴωθε· μᾶλλον δὲ οὐκ αὐτὰ τὰ πράγματα μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ προσδοκίαι ψιλαί· καὶ τί λέγω προσδοκίαι ψιλαί; αἱ σκιαὶ φοβοῦσι καὶ δεδίττουσι τὸν τοιοῦτον· ὁ δὲ ἀποδυσάμενος πάντα, καὶ εἰς τοὺς ἀγῶνας ἐμβὰς, καὶ μυρία δεινὰ παθὼν, ἁπάντων λοιπόν ἐστιν ἀνώτερος, ὥσπερ κολοιῶν κραζόντων, οὕτω τῶν ἀπειλούντων καταγελῶν. Οὐ μικρὸς δὲ οὗτος ὁ στέφανος, οὐδὲ ὁ τυχὼν μισθὸς, ὅταν μηδὲν αὐτὸν τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων δυνήσηται λυπεῖν, ὅταν τὰ τοῖς ἄλλοις φοβερὰ τούτῳ εὐκαταφρόνητα γίνηται, ὅταν ὑπὲρ ὧν ἄλλοι φρίττουσι καὶ ἐξίστανται, ὑπὲρ τούτων μέλλῃ γελᾷν αὐτὸς, τῇ τῆς ὑπομονῆς ὑπερβολῇ εἰς τὴν τῶν ἀγγελικῶν δυνάμεων φιλοσοφίαν ἑαυτὸν μεταστήσας. Εἰ γὰρ δὴ σῶμα μακαρίζομεν τὸ δυνάμενον καὶ ψῦχος καὶ καῦμα ἀλύπως φέρειν, καὶ λιμὸν, καὶ ἔνδειαν, καὶ ὁδοιπορίαν, καὶ ταλαιπωρίας ἑτέρας· πολλῷ μᾶλλον ψυχὴν μακαρίζειν δεῖ τὴν δυναμένην καρτερῶς καὶ γενναίως ἁπάσας τῶν δεινῶν φέρειν τὰς προσβολὰς, καὶ διατηρεῖν ἀδούλωτον αὑτῆς διὰ πάντων τὸ φρόνημα. Ὁ τοιοῦτος τῶν βασιλέων αὐτῶν ἐστι βασιλικώτερος. Ἐκεῖνον μὲν γὰρ καὶ δορυφόροι καὶ φίλοι καὶ ἐχθροὶ πολλὰ δύναιντ' ἂν ἀδικῆσαι ἐπιβουλεύοντες καὶ κακουργοῦντες τὸν δὲ τοιαύτην ἔχοντα ψυχὴν, οἵαν εἶπον νῦν, οὐ βασιλεὺς, οὐ δορυφόρος, οὐκ οἰκέτης, οὐ φίλος, οὐκ ἐχθρὸς, οὐκ αὐτὸς ὁ διάβολος παραβλάψαι δυνήσεται. Πῶς γὰρ, τὸν μελετήσαντα μηδὲν τῶν νομιζομένων εἶναι δεινῶν ἡγεῖσθαι δεινόν; δʹ.
thought_title: The present rewards of virtue's contest
orientation: Chrysostom is arguing that the contest of virtue yields great rewards even before the future resurrection, just as bodily training and long sea voyages yield present gains.
pass_a_gloss: For just as those who compete in the bodily contest, even before the crowns and before the prizes, receive a great reward from the training itself and from the wrestling, making their bodies healthier and stronger through the training, and escaping every illness; so indeed also in the contests of virtue, even before heaven is opened, and before the Son of God arrives, and before we receive the recompenses, we reap a great reward from here, our soul becoming more philosophical. For also those who have sailed much sea, and endured countless waves, and boxed with many beasts, and borne many storms, even before the trading itself reap no small gain from this long journey, by being bold and daring against the sea, and making these overseas journeys fearlessly and with pleasure; so indeed also in the present life, the one who has borne many afflictions for Christ, the one who has suffered many terrible things, even before the kingdom of the heavens received a great recompense, having acquired confidence toward God from here already, and having made his own soul loftier, so as to laugh at all terrible things henceforth. But in order that what is said may become clearer, I want to make it evident by an example. For this very Paul, having endured countless terrible things, received not small recompenses even from here, laughing at tyrants, rising up against raging mobs, despising every punishment, and remaining unshaken toward beasts, and toward iron, and toward seas, and toward cliffs, and toward uprisings, and toward plots, and toward all terrible things; what could be equal to this? For the untrained one who has suffered nothing terrible is accustomed to be disturbed even by chance things; or rather not only by the matters themselves, but also by bare expectations; and why do I say bare expectations? Shadows frighten and terrify such a one; but the one who has stripped off everything, and entered the contests, and suffered countless terrible things, is henceforth above all things, laughing at those who threaten just as at cawing jackdaws. And this is not a small crown, nor a chance reward, when nothing human can grieve him, when the things fearful to others become easily despised by this one, when over the things at which others shudder and are astounded, over these he is about to laugh himself, having transferred himself by the excess of endurance into the philosophy of the angelic powers. For if indeed we bless a body able to bear both cold and heat without pain, and hunger, and want, and journeying, and other hardships; much more must we bless a soul able to bear steadfastly and nobly all the assaults of terrible things, and to keep its purpose unenslaved through all things. Such a one is more kingly than kings themselves. For that one both bodyguards and friends and enemies could wrong in many ways by plotting and doing evil; but the one having such a soul as I just said, neither king, nor bodyguard, nor household servant, nor friend, nor enemy, nor the devil himself will be able to harm. For how, the one who has practiced to consider none of the things thought to be terrible as terrible? 4.

choices.why: Keeps the athletic metaphor of the glossary's 'contest' for ἀγών while distinguishing this from the contest of virtue.
Literal rendering preserves the comparative adjective and the idea of the soul's progressive refinement through virtue.
Literal 'boxed' keeps the athletic metaphor; 'beasts' here means sea monsters or dangers of the deep, not literal animals.

choices.english: to laugh at all terrible things
choices.why: The verb καταγελάω means to laugh down at or mock; keeping 'laugh at' preserves the scornful confidence Chrysostom describes.
The simile compares threats to the noise of jackdaws; 'cawing' conveys the contemptible sound without losing the bird image.
φρόνημα is the mind's resolve or purpose; 'unenslaved' is literal and preserves the freedom-from-domination idea.

pass_b_english: Just as those who compete in a bodily contest receive a great reward even before the crowns and prizes, from the training itself and the wrestling, because they make their bodies healthier and stronger through the exercise and escape every illness, so also in the contests of virtue, even before heaven is opened, before the Son of God arrives, and before we receive our rewards, we already reap a great reward from this, because our soul becomes more philosophical. For those who have sailed a great deal of sea, endured countless waves, fought with many beasts, and borne many storms, even before the trading itself they reap no small profit from this long journey, by being bold and daring against the open sea and making these voyages across the water fearlessly and with pleasure. So also in this present life, the one who has borne many afflictions for Christ, who has suffered many terrible things, has received a great reward even before the kingdom of heaven, having already gained confidence before God from this, and having made his own soul more exalted, so that he now laughs at all terrible things.

To make what I am saying clearer, I want to show it by an example. This very Paul, who endured countless terrible things, received no small rewards even from this: he laughed at tyrants, withstood raging mobs, despised every punishment, and remained unshaken before beasts, iron, seas, cliffs, uprisings, plots, and all terrible things. What could equal this? The untrained person who has suffered nothing terrible is usually disturbed even by ordinary things—or rather, not only by the events themselves, but even by mere expectations. And why do I say mere expectations? Shadows frighten and terrify such a person. But the one who has stripped off everything, entered the contests, and suffered countless terrible things is now above them all, laughing at those who threaten him as if they were cawing jackdaws.

This is no small crown, no ordinary reward: when none of the things of human life can grieve him, when what is fearful to others becomes contemptible to him, when he is about to laugh at the very things that make others shudder and stand amazed, having transferred himself by the excess of his endurance into the philosophy of the angelic powers. For if we bless a body that can bear cold and heat without pain, and hunger, and want, and travel, and other hardships, much more should we bless a soul that can bear all the assaults of terrible things with steadfastness and nobility, and keep its purpose unenslaved through everything. Such a person is more royal than kings themselves. For a king can be wronged in many ways by bodyguards, friends, and enemies who plot against him and do him harm. But the one who has the kind of soul I have just described cannot be harmed by king, bodyguard, servant, friend, enemy, or the devil himself. How could he be, when he has trained himself to consider none of the things thought to be terrible as terrible?

problems.why: πυκτεύω means 'to box/fight,' but 'beasts' here are sea creatures; 'boxed' is absurd
problems.ruling: πυκτεύσαντες with θηρίοις means 'fought beasts'; 'boxed' absurdly narrows πυκτεύω to pugilism against animals.

fixed: Changed 'boxed with many beasts' to 'fought with many sea creatures': πυκτεύω means 'to fight,' and the context is sea travel, so 'beasts' are sea creatures; 'boxed' was absurd.

problems.why: κατεξανιστάμενος means 'rising up against/overthrowing,' but context implies Paul triumphs over mobs, not literally 'rose up' as rebellion.
problems.ruling: κατεξανιστάμενος is middle voice, 'standing firm against,' not active 'rising up against'; 'rose up' wrongly suggests Paul rebelled, reversing agent/patient roles.

problems.why: θηρίοις means beasts/wild animals generally, not specifically sea creatures; the image is boxing against dangers, not marine life.
problems.ruling: θηρίοις means wild beasts generally; context is seafaring dangers, but 'sea creatures' narrows the word's range and misleads readers.

fixed: κατεξανιστάμενος means rising up against/overthrowing; 'overthrew' better captures Paul's triumph over mobs.
θηρίοις means beasts/wild animals generally, not specifically sea creatures; 'beasts' is correct.

problems.ruling: κατεξανιστάμενος means 'standing firm against/withstanding,' not 'overthrew'; changes Paul's action from resistance to destruction.

fixed: Changed 'overthrew raging mobs' to 'withstood raging mobs': κατεξανιστάμενος means 'standing against/withstanding,' not 'overthrowing.'

last_rejected.why: φιλοσοφωτέρας means more devoted to virtue/philosophical in ancient sense, not academic philosophy
last_rejected.fix: more devoted to wisdom, more virtuous
last_rejected.ruling: φιλοσοφωτέρας means more philosophical; in context this implies virtue, not academic error

last_rejected.why: ὑψηλοτέραν here means loftier in virtue/character, not socially exalted
last_rejected.ruling: ὑψηλοτέραν means more exalted; context clarifies moral loftiness, not social rank

last_rejected.why: φιλοσοφίαν here means way of life/virtuous conduct, not intellectual philosophy
last_rejected.fix: way of life, manner of virtue
last_rejected.ruling: φιλοσοφίαν means philosophy; context implies virtuous way of life, not mistranslation

last_rejected.why: μακαρίζομεν means call blessed/happy, not invoke blessing upon
last_rejected.ruling: μακαρίζομεν can mean bless or call blessed; both senses overlap in English usage

last_rejected.why: Same verb: should be call blessed, not bestow blessing
last_rejected.ruling: μακαρίζειν can mean bless or call blessed; both senses overlap in English usage

last_rejected.why: ἀδούλωτον means unenslaved/free, but 'unenslaved' is awkward; 'free' or 'unsubdued' better
last_rejected.ruling: ἀδούλωτον means unenslaved; rendering is accurate, awkwardness is mere preference

last_rejected.why: βασιλικώτερος means more kingly/more fitting for a king, not comparative to kings
last_rejected.fix: more kingly than any king, more truly royal
last_rejected.ruling: βασιλικώτερος with τῶν βασιλέων αὐτῶν naturally reads as comparative; meaning preserved

last_rejected.why: ἀδικῆσαι means harm/injure, not specifically moral wrong; context is physical harm
last_rejected.ruling: ἀδικῆσαι means wrong or harm; 'wronged' covers both, no meaning lost
